finding: No test covers normalizing the stored name (a decomposed NFD name on disk with a composed NFC name typed), so `_fold(name)` on the listed side is unproven
why: Every fixture name is stored as NFC (`\u00e9.md`), so only the typed side is ever normalized; a mutant that sorts by `name.casefold()` for listed names passes the whole suite, even though decomposed stored names are the macOS HFS+ case the delta targets.
fix: Add a case that stores `e\u0301.md` beside a decoy and looks up `\u00c9.md`, expecting `e\u0301.md` (with a pinned listing order).
evidence: Mutant line 590 `for name in sorted(names, key=lambda name: name.casefold() != fold):` -> `13 passed, 73 deselected` under the stored_name / another_case / description_file tests on Windows; fixture `for name in ("0.md", "a.md", "\u00e9.md"):`

finding: The accent-folding assertion in the hard-link test catches a broken fold only when the folder lists its files in a lucky order
why: With samefile patched to always be true, the test checks the preference only when the folder listing puts a decoy name before the expected one; on Linux ext4 the listing is ['é.md', '0.md', 'a.md'], so the expected name comes first and a mutant that drops NFC normalization still passes this assertion (only the Windows CI leg catches it).
fix: Pin the listing order by monkeypatching os.scandir in this test (or mode.os.scandir) so it puts the decoys before the expected entry, giving each assertion a kill that does not depend on the file system.
evidence: Mutant `return name.casefold()` (NFC dropped from _fold, publish_bug_mode.py:600): killed on Windows NTFS (test fails at line 999), but replaying this test's exact logic under WSL python3 on ext4 /tmp gives `nonfc assert1 pass assert2 pass => test passes (mutant SURVIVES)`; listing order seen there in 10 out of 10 trials: ['é.md', '0.md', 'a.md']. tests.yml matrix: ubuntu-latest, windows-latest.
